contexts.context: The excerpt presents patents primarily as signals that reduce information asymmetry between semiconductor start-ups and venture capitalists. Patents provide relatively concrete, time-varying information about a venture’s technical assets and potential, making them especially valuable when investors cannot rely on founders’ prior entrepreneurial experience or reputation. Accordingly, patenting activity is predicted to produce larger upward valuation adjustments for firms with low initial reputation endowments and during earlier financing rounds, when technical and market uncertainty are greatest. As investors learn through site visits, board meetings, and subsequent financing negotiations, the information gap narrows and the incremental signaling value of patents should decline. The signal is also conditional on other reputation resources: start-ups backed by prominent venture capitalists may need patents less to establish quality because those investors can credibly signal quality and provide access to resources, partners, managers, and bankers. For semiconductor firms, the setting allows patents to be studied as instruments that reduce information gaps in private equity markets before any IPO. The excerpt does not fully explain the complementary exclusion-rights function of patents; it mainly supports the quality-signaling side of the dual role. Thus, a complete account of dual value would distinguish patent protection of inventions from patents’ informational effect on VC valuation.

First, patents function as exclusion rights: they certify novel inventions and can help a venture gain competitive advantages, prevent imitation, and protect its technological position. contexts.context: The excerpt describes European novelty as an essentially absolute, first-to-file system. Under the European Patent Convention, the state of the art includes everything made available to the public by written or oral description, use, or any other means before the European application’s filing date. Public accessibility is the central test, and the rule generally does not distinguish between disclosures made by the inventor and those made by third parties, or between different forms or locations of disclosure. Consequently, an inventor’s public disclosure before filing will ordinarily become prior art and can destroy novelty and the ability to obtain a patent in Europe, subject only to narrowly defined statutory exceptions. The excerpt characterizes grace periods in first-to-file systems as exceptions rather than the rule and notes that they are usually short and disclosure-specific; among surveyed systems, six months was more common than one year. By contrast, the U.S. one-year grace period under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(1) is broader in practical effect: certain inventor-originated disclosures, and disclosures derived from the inventor, generally do not defeat a U.S. application filed within one year. Thus, the same pre-filing public disclosure may preserve U.S. patent rights if timely filing follows, but may permanently defeat European rights because Europe generally applies absolute novelty from the filing date.
contexts.question: How does the US one-year grace period under 35 USC 102(b)(1) compare with European absolute novelty requirements? What are the consequences of pre-filing public disclosure for patent rights in the US versus Europe?

contexts.context: The excerpt distinguishes the U.S.-style broad or general grace-period concept from the narrower safety-net approach advocated for Europe. A general grace period can protect various disclosures made during a specified period before filing, potentially including disclosures derived from the inventor and priority claims. By contrast, a safety-net grace period is limited to protecting an inventor from the novelty-destroying effect of the inventor’s own disclosure. The article argues that this limited protection would preserve the first-to-file structure while helping unsophisticated applicants, university researchers, and small and medium-sized enterprises. The European Patent Convention is described as lacking such a safety net and as having rejected the broader general grace period because it is incompatible with first-to-file systems. Thus, the excerpt supports the conclusion that a pre-filing public disclosure may destroy patent novelty in Europe unless a narrowly defined exception applies, whereas the U.S. one-year rule is broader and can preserve patentability for qualifying disclosures made within the statutory period. contexts.context: The excerpt explains the U.S. transition from the pre-AIA first-to-invent system to the America Invents Act’s first-inventor-to-file framework. Under the former regime, a twelve-month grace period could protect an inventor from the inventor’s own disclosure and, in some circumstances, from an independent third party’s disclosure when the inventor could establish an earlier invention date. The AIA instead uses the application’s effective filing date to determine prior art, eliminating uncertainty associated with disputes over invention dates. It generally removes protection against independent, non-derived third-party disclosures made before that filing date; such subject matter constitutes prior art. The amended statute also includes an “otherwise available to the public” category, and the excerpt states that all acts making an invention available to the public can qualify as prior art. At the same time, the amended section 102(b) is described as providing a one-year grace period, with the precise interpretation still discussed at the time of writing, including congressional statements suggesting protection for an inventor’s own disclosure and disclosures of the same subject matter by others. The excerpt does not discuss European patent law or absolute novelty requirements, so it cannot establish the European consequences of pre-filing disclosure or provide a direct US-Europe comparison.

contexts.context: The excerpt contrasts the US system’s statutory one-year grace period with the generally stricter European approach, where grace-period provisions vary substantially and many countries effectively require absolute novelty by avoiding a grace period. Under 35 USC 102(b)(1), an inventor may publicly disclose an invention and still file a US application within one year; disclosures such as publication, public use, or an offer for sale made more than one year before filing will preclude US patenting. The US protection is not unlimited: the AIA grace period primarily covers disclosures of the same subject matter that originated with the inventor, and a third party’s disclosure of a variation or improvement may still constitute prior art against the inventor. In Europe, a pre-filing public disclosure generally destroys novelty and therefore can eliminate patent rights, unless a particular national or regional exception applies. The differing rules create uncertainty for applicants seeking international protection: a disclosure preserved by the US grace period may already be fatal in European jurisdictions. The article also identifies provisional applications as an alternative US strategy, allowing an initial filing after disclosure within the one-year period and providing a priority date, while a nonprovisional application must be filed before the 12-month pendency expires.

contexts.context: The excerpt contrasts the US approach after the America Invents Act with the generally stricter European approach. Under the US system, the first-inventor-to-file framework preserves a one-year grace period: an inventor’s public disclosure does not necessarily destroy patent rights if a patent application is filed within one year of that disclosure. This gives US inventors a limited period to proceed with filing after disclosure. European patent law generally follows an absolute-novelty principle and, apart from narrow exceptions in the European Patent Convention (EPC), does not provide a comparable grace period. Consequently, an inventor who makes an invention publicly available before filing will ordinarily lose the ability to obtain European patent protection. The EPC exceptions are limited: disclosure may be disregarded when it occurred within six months before filing and resulted from an evident abuse against the applicant or from displaying the invention at an official or officially recognized international exhibition. Some European countries provide additional or longer national protections, including 12-month periods in Estonia and Turkey, but the excerpt emphasizes substantial variation and the lack of harmonization. Thus, pre-filing disclosure is potentially survivable in the US during the one-year grace period, while in Europe it is generally fatal unless a narrowly defined exception applies.
contexts.question: How does the US one-year grace period under 35 USC 102(b)(1) compare with European absolute novelty requirements? What are the consequences of pre-filing public disclosure for patent rights in the US versus Europe?

contexts.context: The excerpt contrasts the comparatively broad U.S. safety-net approach under the America Invents Act with Europe’s generally strict absolute-novelty regime. In the United States, a qualifying pre-filing disclosure can be addressed through the statutory grace-period framework. The applicant does not have to invoke the grace period when filing; instead, the applicant may identify it in the specification and later provide documentation to overcome a rejection based on the earlier disclosure or to disqualify an intervening third-party disclosure. The cited examination guidance also indicates that protection may extend where intervening disclosure of the same subject matter is not verbatim, including a general description of subject matter previously disclosed. Thus, a U.S. inventor’s own public disclosure does not necessarily destroy patentability if the statutory grace-period conditions are met, although the excerpt emphasizes that the statute is not intended to restore patentability after an unrelated inventor independently publishes the same invention or an obvious variation. By contrast, Europe has no general grace period under the European Patent Convention: public disclosure ordinarily defeats novelty, even when the applicant was unaware of or unable to comply with the requirement. Article 55 recognizes only narrow six-month exceptions, including third-party “evident abuse,” requiring intent to cause harm or constructive knowledge that harm could result.

contexts.context: The excerpt frames patent-paper pairs as one of four possible disclosure regimes for research projects that produce both commercially useful applications and scientific knowledge. A firm may choose secrecy, publication (“open science”), patenting without publication (“commercial science”), or both patenting and academic publication (“patent-paper pairs”). The paper’s central theoretical problem is the negotiation between scientists’ preferences for publication-based scientific rewards and firms’ concerns about competition, commercial value, and intellectual-property protection. It rejects a simple assumption that industry research necessarily leads to patents while academic research leads to publications: universities may patent, industrial scientists may publish, and a single project can generate multiple disclosure outcomes. The model therefore treats disclosure as an endogenous choice linked to scientists’ publication preferences and the firm’s commercial environment. The excerpt indicates that the relationship between publication rights and patenting depends on the effects of disclosure on competition and future licensing. However, these pages do not provide the detailed mechanism for how patent-paper pairs are implemented, nor do they specify the precise timing or sequencing rules governing patent filing and academic publication. They establish only that patenting and publishing can be jointly selected and that their interaction is a core subject of the formal model.
contexts.question: How do patent-paper pairs work? How do academic researchers manage the tension between publishing scientific results and filing patents? What is the relationship between academic publication and patent filing timing?

contexts.context: The excerpt treats patent-paper pairs as arrangements in which a research team’s scientific publication and patent filing are jointly determined through negotiation between scientists and firms. The central tension is that publication can disclose information and potentially weaken the value or bargaining position associated with intellectual property, while also generating recognition (“kudos”) and, in some circumstances, accelerating research. If scientists own the relevant IP, previously published scientists may accept lower future licensing fees because later generations can affect the value of their recognition. This lowers the effective return to publication for the current team and narrows the circumstances in which patent-paper pairs or open-science outcomes arise compared with firm ownership. The excerpt also links publication to timing: when research effort or intensity is not contractible, the firm can use permission for a sufficient level of disclosure as an incentive for scientists to complete research sooner rather than later. Thus, publication may be accepted even when it is not independently surplus-enhancing, because it motivates timely research. In competitive races, teams compete to complete research first; the first firm obtains the patent, while simultaneous completion gives each an equal chance. These mechanisms imply that patent filing and academic publication are connected to bargaining, disclosure incentives, priority competition, and the timing of research completion rather than being entirely separate decisions.
contexts.question: How do patent-paper pairs work? How do academic researchers manage the tension between publishing scientific results and filing patents? What is the relationship between academic publication and patent filing timing?

contexts.context: Patent-paper pairs involve disclosing related scientific knowledge through both a patent and a scholarly publication. The excerpt presents this as a common and deliberate strategy among firms, academics, and technology licensing officers, rather than an accidental overlap. Examples include researchers whose patented discoveries are also described in papers, sometimes with the paper providing no additional disclosure beyond the patent. The strategy reflects a tension between scientists’ preference for rapid publication—because publication establishes intellectual priority, generates credit and citations, and supports academic or industrial careers—and firms’ interest in protecting commercially valuable results and maximizing profits. Academic researchers and universities can manage this tension by coordinating patenting and publication, generally ensuring that a patent application is filed before public disclosure in a paper. Timing is legally important: under the U.S. rule described in the excerpt, if publication precedes patent filing by more than one year, the publication becomes prior art and can invalidate the patent. Thus, pursuing both outputs requires advance planning, often using the patent application to secure protection before publishing the scientific findings. The excerpt also notes that universities are incentivized to patent research to promote dissemination, although scientists may worry that intellectual-property protection can interfere with scientific norms and follow-on research.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents patent-paper pairs as a disclosure regime in which a patent filing and an academic publication coexist, rather than requiring researchers to choose exclusively between secrecy, patenting without publication, or open science. Firms and scientists negotiate the level of publication disclosure because publishing can reveal information that affects competitors and may reduce future licensing revenues. Stronger patent protection raises the value of patenting and, on the intensive margin, can allow or induce more extensive publication rights. When future licensing concerns are weak, or patents effectively protect future returns, patents and publications are complements: stronger patent protection increases incentives to patent and reinforces publication. When future licensing concerns are substantial, however, patenting and publication may be substitutes, since publication can undermine licensing revenues; the overall effect on publication is then ambiguous. Patent disclosure requirements also have competing effects: they can make publication easier by reducing duplicated disclosure costs, but they increase the cost of patenting and may encourage secrecy. The passage does not provide a precise legal or empirical rule for the timing of filing versus publication, but it implies that patenting and publication are coordinated through contractual negotiation, with patent strength and disclosure requirements shaping how much and through which pathway scientific results are disclosed.

contexts.context: Patent-paper pairs are a disclosure strategy in which one research project produces knowledge relevant both to scientific inquiry and to useful commercial or technical applications. Researchers disclose the work through two institutional channels: a peer-reviewed academic paper, which makes the findings available to the scientific community, and a patent, which provides intellectual-property protection for the invention. The excerpt describes these disclosures as potentially simultaneous, allowing researchers to obtain patent rights while preserving publication and future scientific use. The content of the patent and paper can vary in overlap. In some cases, the paper reports a fundamental scientific breakthrough while the patent covers an immediate application; in other cases, the two documents disclose highly congruent or nearly identical knowledge. More generally, academic publication is supported by scientific institutions such as peer review and provides reputation and career benefits, whereas patenting creates incentives by protecting against imitation and requires disclosure sufficient for a skilled person to replicate the invention. Thus, the apparent tension between publishing and patenting can be managed when the project supports both objectives, with the patent and paper serving complementary roles. This excerpt specifically indicates simultaneous disclosure but does not provide detailed contractual rules or a full account of priority deadlines and sequencing beyond that timing relationship.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes patent-paper pairs as coordinated outputs of the same research: a firm’s scientist may prepare a scientific paper while lawyers or intellectual-property specialists determine whether the underlying discovery is patentable. Firms commonly conduct an internal review before publication to identify intellectual property, prevent unwanted knowledge spillovers, and selectively disclose only what can safely be revealed. If patentable subject matter is found, the patent application is generally prepared before the paper is submitted, creating a trade-off between rapid academic disclosure and protection of the invention. The Genentech example illustrates this sequencing, with scientists consulting patent attorneys before presenting or submitting work and filing applications before sending papers. Publication can also establish prior art and trigger a one-year USPTO filing deadline, which may force a firm to patent before it is strategically ready to disclose the invention. Thus, publication and patent filing are closely linked but temporally sensitive: filing first protects novelty and appropriation, while publication can provide scientific visibility and credibility but may expose the invention to competitors and constrain later patenting. The process requires substantial coordination among scientists, lawyers, and internal reviewers.

contexts.context: The excerpt defines a patent-paper pair as the equilibrium outcome in which a patent is filed (i = 1) and scientific disclosure or publication occurs (d > 0). The model distinguishes this outcome from secrecy (no patent and no disclosure), commercial science (a patent without disclosure), and open science (disclosure without a patent). Researchers manage the publication–patenting tension through negotiated disclosure: when patenting occurs, disclosure can be sufficiently high while the scientist’s wage is driven to zero. Because publication eliminates wage payments, additional commercial surplus created by patent protection can instead be transferred to the scientist through greater permitted disclosure. The excerpt therefore presents patents and publication as potentially complementary rather than inherently conflicting. Stronger patent protection increases commercial returns and makes patenting more likely; in turn, this can increase the likelihood and level of publication. The passage does not provide a detailed chronology for whether filing must precede publication or specify an exact filing-to-publication interval. It does, however, indicate that the patent decision and negotiated disclosure level are jointly determined, and that stronger patent rights can encourage published disclosures in commercially funded academic research. Publishing can help firms recruit scientific talent by signaling research capabilities, especially when AI scientists have strong bargaining power. contexts.context: The excerpt presents the Bayh-Dole Act of 1980 as the principal policy intervention behind the emergence of university technology transfer offices (TTOs). For federally funded research, the Act shifted ownership of resulting inventions and other intellectual property from the federal government to universities, small businesses, and nonprofit organizations, provided recipients satisfy specified conditions. These include actively promoting commercialization, protecting inventions through patents or comparable mechanisms, compensating inventors through royalty sharing, favoring domestic industry and small businesses, claiming title within a prescribed period, and disclosing inventions to the funding agency. contexts.context: The excerpt portrays the Bayh-Dole Act as establishing a limited and somewhat ambiguous framework for university technology transfer: it requires universities to facilitate commercialization of federally supported inventions and favors domestic and small businesses, but does not require technology diffusion at any cost. Technology transfer offices (TTOs) therefore exercise substantial judgment in managing intellectual property and structuring licenses. Their responsibilities include encouraging development and use, setting milestones for exclusive licensees, requiring sublicensing where appropriate, keeping research tools broadly accessible, and scrutinizing licenses to patent aggregators. TTOs are also expected to reserve rights for university research and for nonprofit or governmental users, while avoiding license provisions—such as unnecessary claims over future improvements—that could restrict inventors’ research, collaboration, publication, or access to future funding. The excerpt suggests that universities balance publication and patent protection by preserving the ability to perform and publish related research and by limiting exclusivity when it could obstruct further research or unanticipated uses. Exclusive rights are considered justified primarily when substantial investment is needed for development and broad implementation. Finally, TTOs monitor closed agreements and enforce intellectual-property rights selectively, weighing prosecution against research relationships, industrial sponsorship, and the broader goal of effective technology transfer. The overall priority is societal deployment and academic impact rather than maximizing licensing revenue.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents the Bayh-Dole Act as a formal regulatory force that changed the institutional environment for academic technology transfer. After universities were subject to such regulation, they increasingly relied on professionalization—particularly the development of specialized personnel and practices—to manage technology-transfer activities. Technology transfer offices (TTOs) became widespread across research universities in the United States and Europe, partly through imitation of prominent models at MIT and Stanford and partly because they helped universities gain legitimacy, resources, networks, and commercialization capabilities. The passage does not detail specific Bayh-Dole ownership or licensing provisions, but it links the Act to the institutionalization and professionalization of university technology transfer. Managing intellectual property is presented alongside a tension between patenting and academic priorities. Potential drawbacks include delayed publication, secrecy, reduced data sharing, diversion of research and teaching resources, and constraints on future research caused by exclusive patent rights. However, several cited studies find that patenting and publication can be complementary rather than substitutive, with entrepreneurial activity sometimes associated with greater publication output and no decline in research quality. Thus, the excerpt portrays universities as balancing IP protection and dissemination through professionalized TTO structures while negotiating competing norms of commercialization and open science.
contexts.question: How does the Bayh-Dole Act affect university technology transfer? What role do technology transfer offices play in managing IP from federally funded research? How do universities balance publication with patent protection?

contexts.context: The excerpt frames open-source participation as potentially valuable to startups through two mechanisms: improving technology and increasing visibility to investors. The authors explicitly investigate whether engagement with open-source communities (OSCs) helps startups achieve funding milestones, whether effects differ across technologies, and which investors are most sensitive to such activity. Their empirical strategy links Crunchbase startup financing and investor data with GitHub organization accounts and time-stamped public events from GHArchive. They identify engagement with external repositories—especially forks—as the primary measure of OSC participation. Forking enables startups to copy and build on existing code, supporting knowledge sharing, collaboration, and internal technology development. The data suggest that startups’ GitHub activity is predominantly development-oriented: 96% of external interactions are forks, while watches and pushes account for only 2% and 1%, respectively. This pattern implies that open-source activity may signal substantive technological upgrading rather than merely public commenting or promotional disclosure. The study also classifies external repositories into software development/backend, machine learning, APIs, and user interfaces, finding that startups most often engage with software development/backend and API repositories. Although the excerpt does not report the funding results, it establishes how open code-sharing is measured and why it could attract venture capital by demonstrating technical capabilities, development effort, and participation in collaborative technology ecosystems.
contexts.question: How does open-source participation or open disclosure of technology attract venture capital investment? Can startups benefit from sharing code, designs, or data openly? Evidence from GitHub and open source hardware startups.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide direct evidence that open-source participation or disclosure attracts venture-capital investment, nor does it discuss GitHub-based fundraising or investor reactions. It does, however, identify mechanisms through which open sharing can improve a startup’s credibility, market access, and commercial prospects—factors that may indirectly support investment readiness. Openly publishing a design can demonstrate technological capability to potential clients and collaborators: Trillion Technology open-sourced a 3D-printable telescope to attract NASA and other space-agency collaborations, with the founder explaining that showing something real helps the world understand the firm’s capabilities. Open disclosure can also function as a business-model strategy: firms may release designs while earning higher-margin revenue from consulting, training, customization, cloud software, and related services. In open-source hardware markets, disclosure may be necessary to reach early adopters who demand autonomy and control, particularly in education, DIY, robotics, microcontroller, and 3D-printer markets. The excerpt further suggests that openness can accelerate product launch, reduce presales investment and go-to-market time, and enable community innovation. These benefits could make a startup more attractive to investors by providing visible proof of capability, customer traction, partnerships, and scalable complementary revenues, but that investor-attraction inference is not directly tested in the cited passage.
contexts.question: How does open-source participation or open disclosure of technology attract venture capital investment? Can startups benefit from sharing code, designs, or data openly? Evidence from GitHub and open source hardware startups.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that open-source participation can help startups attract venture funding, but its value depends strongly on the startup’s technology and competitive environment. Startups developing relatively novel technologies were more likely to engage with open-source communities on GitHub, and after doing so were eight percentage points more likely to have attracted funding than other startups that engaged with such communities. The likely logic is that open-source interaction provides relatively cheap and readily available technological input, helping novel-technology startups solve complex development problems and move rapidly toward market leadership. However, open disclosure can create appropriability concerns when many startups use the same technology. Startups in highly competitive markets were 14 percentage points less likely to have been financed after engaging with open-source communities; the estimated overall funding effect in such markets was zero. The study also uses the 2014 availability of GitHub Enterprise through AWS as a shock that lowered the relative cost of developing proprietary software. Startups sharply reduced public GitHub engagement afterward, while the relationship between open-source engagement and funding became stronger. This suggests that startups selectively share or use open source when its expected benefits—such as development assistance, collaboration, or signaling—are large enough to outweigh disclosure and opportunity costs. The excerpt provides evidence for software startups, not directly for open-source hardware or all forms of openly shared designs and data.
contexts.question: How does open-source participation or open disclosure of technology attract venture capital investment? Can startups benefit from sharing code, designs, or data openly? Evidence from GitHub and open source hardware startups.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides evidence that open-source participation can attract venture capital through both signaling and substantive technology development. Using a difference-in-differences design comparing startups engaged with external GitHub repositories to matched startups, the authors find that external open-source engagement is associated with at least a 36% increase in the likelihood of receiving funding. The relationship is strongest for startups developing novel technologies, where access to external knowledge and collaboration may help offset appropriability concerns, and weakest in highly competitive settings where protecting intellectual property is more important. AI and Blockchain startups benefit particularly strongly, potentially because open source helps bring complex technologies to market faster. The evidence suggests that investors value more than mere online visibility: startups gain from interacting with repositories across software/backend, machine learning, APIs, and user interfaces, and engagement is linked to product launches and completion of at least a minimum viable product. Investors do not respond to purely cosmetic README changes, supporting a knowledge-production rather than simple publicity explanation. The association is especially strong for venture capital and successful investors, who are more likely to value underlying technology. The excerpt does not provide evidence specifically about open-source hardware startups, designs, or data, so those implications remain unestablished here.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides empirical evidence that open-source participation can improve startups’ ability to attract financing. Using a difference-in-differences design comparing startups that begin engaging with external GitHub repositories to matched, non-engaged controls, the authors find that GitHub-engaged startups are 15 percentage points more likely to have raised a financing round, equivalent to a 65% increase over the control-group outcome mean. The estimated effect remains positive under progressively stricter fixed effects, declining to 12 percentage points and then 8 percentage points when accounting for industry-by-year effects and startup age-by-firm effects. The absence of meaningful pre-treatment differences supports the interpretation that funding likelihood rises after open-source engagement; the relationship is described as strong, immediate, and persistent. Additional analysis distinguishes external open-source interaction from use of a startup’s own internal GitHub repositories. Engagement with external repositories is associated with funding at a rate nine percentage points higher than internal-repository activity, suggesting the result is not merely driven by general technology development or lifecycle effects. The excerpt therefore supports the argument that sharing or collaborating around code publicly may signal capability, accelerate development, and make startups more attractive to investors. It does not provide direct evidence here about open hardware, designs, or data disclosure.
contexts.question: How does open-source participation or open disclosure of technology attract venture capital investment? Can startups benefit from sharing code, designs, or data openly? Evidence from GitHub and open source hardware startups.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides empirical evidence that startup participation in open-source communities can improve access to venture capital. The researchers link 160,065 U.S. startups in Crunchbase with their public activity on GitHub and compare startups that begin engaging with external repositories against otherwise similar firms matched by founding year, location, technology, and human capital. Their difference-in-differences results indicate that GitHub open-source engagement is associated with at least a 36% increase in the likelihood of receiving funding. The proposed mechanism is not simply signaling openness: open-source participation gives startups access to external knowledge and developer communities that can help improve their technology and reach a minimum viable product. This can make a young venture more investment-ready by accelerating production, progress, connections, and technology development. contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide direct evidence that open-source participation attracts venture capital investment, nor does it discuss GitHub-based funding signals or investor decision-making. It does, however, identify mechanisms through which open disclosure can make startups more investable or economically attractive. Open source may reduce the burden of patent filing and protection, which is particularly important for cash-sensitive hardware startups. Sharing designs can also lower product-iteration costs by enabling communities to search for solutions, prototype, test, and co-develop products when founders lack technical capabilities or access to talent. Open documentation and source files may reduce customer-support costs because technically skilled users can diagnose and repair problems themselves; companies can update software through repositories such as GitHub. Strategically, openness gives firms access to user innovations and feedback, helping them identify product improvements and emerging applications. It can also help startups educate nascent markets, establish technical standards, build reputation, encourage ecosystem participation, and create future revenue opportunities through services and consultancy. Thus, the excerpt supports an indirect investment case: sharing code, designs, and related technical information can demonstrate community traction, accelerate validation, lower costs, and build market position. These benefits could improve fundraising prospects, but the source does not establish a causal relationship with venture capital investment.

contexts.context: The excerpt suggests that open-source participation can attract venture capital by making a startup’s technological development more visible and credible to investors. Public GitHub activity may be reviewed during investor due diligence, allowing investors to observe evidence of development effort, technology choices, and progress rather than relying only on private claims or business plans. The paper’s central conclusion is that using open-source components to build at least a minimum viable product can help startups reach funding milestones. Open sourcing therefore appears to function as an early-stage signal: it opens the technology “black-box,” demonstrates that the founders have made concrete tech-stack investments, and may help reduce information frictions between startups and investors. The excerpt also frames open-source engagement as external knowledge acquisition that can improve startup performance outcomes. However, it cautions that the evidence is based on activities on GitHub, a specific online platform, so external validity may be limited. The passage does not provide direct evidence about open-source hardware startups, nor does it establish that publicly sharing all code, designs, or data universally increases funding; the supported claim is narrower—that visible GitHub activity and open-source development, particularly sufficient to produce a minimum viable product, can help attract funding, especially for early-stage technology ventures.

The relationship is especially strong for larger funding rounds and for financing from venture capitalists and successful investors, who can provide substantial non-financial capital. GitHub engagement is also associated with launching new, particularly high-quality, technology products, implying that open-source inputs help startups access external knowledge, scale, integrate with broader ecosystems, and develop a minimum viable product. The strongest benefits occur for novel technologies, including AI and blockchain, where shared algorithms, packages, and community contributions can offset the costs of disclosure. The findings do not support visibility alone as the main mechanism: investors reportedly do not respond to cosmetic improvements to repository README files. Instead, startups appear to benefit when open disclosure reflects genuine development and use of community knowledge. The excerpt provides evidence from GitHub-based software startups, but does not directly address open-source hardware startups or the effects of openly sharing physical designs or data.
contexts.question: How does open-source participation or open disclosure of technology attract venture capital investment? Can startups benefit from sharing code, designs, or data openly? Evidence from GitHub and open source hardware startups.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides a general framework for understanding IP and appropriability risks in university spin-outs, but it does not specifically discuss open disclosure, investors, or the technical protection challenges of materials, chemistry, and manufacturing startups. It argues that appropriability is partly endogenous: entrepreneurs choose between investing in control-based protection, such as formal intellectual property, and investing in rapid execution and commercialization. These choices are strategic substitutes because control can delay commercialization, while execution can help a venture move ahead of competitors but may leave it more exposed to imitation or loss of control. The relevant uncertainty is Rosenbergian uncertainty—the difficulty of predicting how a successful invention will ultimately be used and commercialized. Since the size and probability of future rents are uncertain, entrepreneurs may not be able to determine in advance whether control or execution is superior; decisions may instead reflect preferences, capabilities, and overall strategy. Evidence from academic ventures shows that faculty-led spin-outs are more associated with formal IP, whereas student-led ventures commercialize more rapidly and exhibit a trade-off between patenting and speed. This suggests that university spin-outs face a fundamental tension between preserving exclusivity through formal IP and disclosing or deploying technology quickly enough to establish market position. The excerpt does not identify specific requirements for protecting trade secrets, patentable formulations, process know-how, or manufacturing methods.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes open-source hardware as a way to capture value indirectly rather than primarily through exclusive rights over designs. Firms can use openness to reduce product-development costs by recruiting communities for searching, prototyping, testing, and co-development. They can also lower customer-support costs because technically capable users and community members may diagnose and repair products themselves. Entrepreneurs who do not patent may choose openness because patent filing is expensive, slow, and poorly matched to rapidly changing hardware markets; they may prefer public experimentation and iteration over protecting uncertain inventions. Other strategies include using open designs to gain user innovation, identify product improvements, and learn from derivative products. Firms can also educate nascent markets, establish technical standards, build reputation, and attract future customers. Value may then come from complementary offerings such as consultancy, technological and legal services, or other support around the open platform. The main risks indicated are that competitors or customers can copy the product and that openness may reduce direct exclusivity. However, reciprocal licenses such as GPL can require users of the design and code to open their own modifications, preserving access to improvements. The benefits therefore include faster innovation, community participation, lower costs, market development, and service-based revenue, while risks include imitation and reliance on indirect commercialization.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes several ways open-source hardware firms capture value despite sharing designs. Entrepreneurs may sell the physical product at a low margin while earning more from complementary services such as coaching, training, outsourcing, incubation, customization, consulting, and cloud software. Open designs can also function as demonstrations of technical capability, helping firms attract clients, collaboration, or institutional partners. In some markets—especially education, DIY, robotics, microcontrollers, and 3D printing—customers expect openness because they want autonomy, customization, learning, and control; sharing designs is therefore a market-entry strategy. Entrepreneurs may also be required to use open licenses when building on GPL-licensed modules, or adopt openness to serve niche markets whose ideology favors sharing. The excerpt identifies cost and speed benefits: open licensing can reduce presales investment and shorten time to market, which is particularly important for cash-constrained hardware startups. Avoiding patents can be rational where patents are slow, expensive, technologically weak, or unable to prevent reverse engineering. However, openness creates exposure to copying and imitation, while proprietary closure may exclude some customers and limit user innovation. The potential benefits include community assistance, user-driven improvements, market access, credibility, collaboration, and faster iteration; the principal risks are low hardware margins, imitation, and dependence on complementary revenue streams.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides partial insight into how open-source hardware entrepreneurs may capture value without relying exclusively on patents. It identifies three extrinsic motivations tied to business value: expanding market demand, reducing development costs, and strengthening the firm’s brand. These suggest that openly sharing designs can support commercialization indirectly through broader adoption, lower development expenses, and reputational or branding benefits. The excerpt also describes community-based value: sharing can attract like-minded collaborators, generate feedback and ideas, and increase reputation within a community. Intrinsic motivations may coexist with or substitute for conventional financial returns. Some founders shared designs for enjoyment, learning, community participation, or modest income, and self-enjoyment-oriented entrepreneurs often had another source of livelihood and began open-source activity before acquiring their first purchaser. Altruistic examples show additional benefits involving affordable products, improved accessibility, and democratization of technologies that were otherwise expensive or controlled by large firms. However, this passage does not directly explain specific value-capture mechanisms such as selling hardware, services, manufacturing, licensing, or complementary products; nor does it explicitly discuss patent avoidance, competitive risks, imitation, appropriation, or disclosure risks. Therefore, it supports broad benefits and motivations for open approaches but is insufficient for a complete account of strategy or risk.

contexts.context: The excerpt is primarily a bibliography rather than a discussion of findings, but it identifies several sources directly relevant to understanding value capture and strategy in open-source hardware. Pearce (2017) addresses “Emerging business models for open source hardware,” while Pearce (2015) examines how to quantify the value created by open-source hardware development. Howard et al. (2012) considers business models associated with open design and crowdsourcing. The references also point to research on whether property rights remain important when commercializing open technologies (Mann 2006), how firms use selective revealing in open innovation (Henkel, Schöberl & Alexy 2014), and how open design relates to user entrepreneurship (Shah & Tripsas 2007). Other cited works concern collaboration, collective innovation, communities, and the motivations for participating in open-source projects, including Hars and Ou (2002), Kyriakou and Nickerson (2014), and Mellis and Buechley (2012). Thus, these pages provide leads to literature on business models, intellectual-property strategy, community-based production, and the economic value of openness, but they do not themselves describe specific mechanisms, risks, or benefits in enough detail to support firm conclusions.

contexts.context: The excerpt frames open-source hardware (OSH) entrepreneurship as a departure from the conventional strategy of patenting designs to exclude imitators and capture commercial value. Instead, OSH entrepreneurs license product designs and technologies under open-source terms, allowing the public to use them for free and sharing designs online with communities organized around technological or social interests. The passage does not yet specify the firms’ detailed value-capture mechanisms, but it establishes that value creation and value capture are central themes of the study and that open licensing is a deliberate alternative to proprietary protection. Conventional intellectual-property theory predicts that patents provide market power by preventing other firms from using the technology, which is particularly important for resource-constrained startups facing imitation. Open approaches therefore expose entrepreneurs to risks associated with imitation, uncertainty, and difficulty appropriating returns from pioneering investments. At the same time, the excerpt identifies potential benefits: access to global maker communities, participation in collaborative and transdisciplinary innovation, and the possibility of turning shared projects into commercial products. The existence and rapid revenue growth of firms such as SparkFun and Ultimaker demonstrate that open hardware can support viable businesses, although the excerpt does not identify the specific operational strategies used to generate those revenues.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents tacit knowledge as highly important to university technology transfer because patents and licensing alone do not convey all of the practical, experience-based knowledge needed to develop university inventions commercially. Additional mechanisms are therefore necessary alongside patent licensing. These include professional and social networks, consulting, sponsored research, corporate positions, and more integrated institutional relationships. Their common feature is repeated, interpersonal, practice-oriented interaction, which enables academic and industry personnel to exchange uncodified knowledge and develop the absorptive capacity needed to apply new discoveries. For spin-offs and other commercial partners, ongoing relationships with academic inventors can therefore be essential beyond the patent itself: networks may initiate contact, while consulting, collaborative research, advice, or direct corporate involvement permit more intensive knowledge exchange. The faculty inventor plays a practical commercialization role by explaining and transferring know-how, helping firms understand and exploit the invention, and remaining involved after licensing. The excerpt specifically reports that academic inventor involvement increases both the likelihood that a technology will be commercialized and the royalties it generates. It also indicates that companies value broad academic engagement—including consulting, collaborative and contract research, ad hoc advice, and networking—more highly than university patent licensing alone.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents tacit knowledge as a central, often indispensable component of university-industry technology transfer, rather than a minor supplement to patents and licenses. Although patents formally disclose inventions, important practical and commercialization knowledge remains uncodified and resides in the faculty inventor. This knowledge may include experiential know-how, heuristics, rules of thumb, and other “tricks of the trade” needed both to practice an invention and to adapt it into a viable commercial product. Consequently, patent licensing alone often fails to provide a commercial partner with everything required for successful development. Spin-offs, like other technology-transfer mechanisms, need continuing human and institutional connections with academic inventors; direct interpersonal interaction is generally necessary to identify, communicate, and apply knowledge that cannot be fully written down. The faculty inventor therefore plays a crucial role beyond inventing and securing patent protection: they act as a source of practical guidance and tacit expertise, helping transferees understand, reproduce, refine, and commercialize the technology. The excerpt specifically identifies university spin-offs, consulting engagements, corporate positions, sponsored research, proof-of-concept centers, incubators, and networks as mechanisms that can sustain or facilitate this knowledge transfer.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents tacit knowledge as central to university technology transfer because inventors possess experiential know-how, rules of thumb, procedures, and practical judgment that are difficult to articulate or reproduce from written materials alone. This is especially important in biotechnology, where biological inventions may not be predictably reproducible solely from a patent or academic publication. Consequently, transferring a university invention to a private firm for development and commercialization is complicated by knowledge that remains with the academic inventor. Patents do not eliminate this problem: although applicants must satisfy enablement and written-description requirements, patent documents may contain knowledge gaps, omit detailed production specifications, rely on experimentation, and use jargon that obscures practical information. The excerpt specifically indicates that commercialization-relevant knowledge must be supplied through human interactions, implying that spin-offs and other technology recipients need continuing access to the faculty inventor or other knowledgeable researchers beyond the patent document. The faculty inventor therefore serves not merely as the creator of the patented invention but also as a source of practical know-how needed to interpret, reproduce, adapt, and further develop it. Tacitness varies by degree, including latent knowledge that could be codified but remains uncodified because codification is costly or incentives are lacking.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents tacit knowledge as an important element of university-industry technology transfer, particularly because it supports the practical development and commercialization of inventions that may be too embryonic to patent or license effectively. Sponsored research enables continuing relationships between corporations and faculty inventors, joint work between academic and corporate scientists, embedded corporate researchers, and institutional arrangements that blur university-industry boundaries. These sustained interactions facilitate the exchange of technical knowledge that is difficult to capture in patents. Proof-of-concept centers and incubators extend this process: mentors and technical advisors transfer tacit technical knowledge to industry while also providing faculty inventors with tacit business and commercialization knowledge. Incubators promote working relationships between academic scientists and entrepreneurs, and research parks increase opportunities for informal knowledge exchange through institutional and geographic proximity. Thus, the faculty inventor is not merely the creator of a patented invention; continued access to the inventor’s expertise, relationships, and practical know-how can be central to commercialization. The excerpt ends just as it begins discussing university spinoffs, so it does not provide specific details about the ongoing interaction requirements of spinoffs beyond the broader evidence that commercialization depends on sustained inventor-industry contact.

contexts.context: Tacit knowledge is central to university technology transfer because academic inventions are typically novel, complex, embryonic, and insufficiently developed for immediate commercial use. Most university inventions are proofs of concept or laboratory-scale prototypes at licensing, while only a small share are ready for practical or commercial application. Consequently, patents alone generally do not provide all the knowledge needed to practice an invention, scale it, manufacture it, or turn it into a marketable product. The faculty inventor contributes practical, action-oriented know-how that fills the gap between patent disclosure, laboratory operation, and commercial production. For spin-offs and other licensees, this role extends beyond receiving static information: they may need continuing access to the inventor’s specialized expertise and dynamic problem-solving abilities. Ongoing interaction is especially important when production processes are not fully specified, as in biotechnology, where scientists and engineers must work together to preserve product integrity during scale-up. Faculty inventors are uniquely positioned to diagnose commercialization challenges, adapt the technology beyond its basic form, and transfer useful experiential “tidbits” that cannot easily be codified. Effective commercialization therefore depends on sustained interpersonal exchange between academic inventors and firms, not merely on the formal patent transaction.

contexts.context: The excerpt portrays tacit knowledge as essential to university technology transfer because a patent is only a formal document assigning usage rights and does not capture the inventor’s full, experience-based understanding of the technology. Effective commercialization therefore requires continuing personal interaction between the academic inventor and the people developing and promoting the business. The inventor remains the ultimate technical expert, while TTO staff need enough understanding to identify important features and applications without attempting to replace the inventor’s depth of knowledge. This interaction may continue through different roles, including active participation as a member of a spin-off’s staff or management, or a more limited position on a scientific advisory board. Spin-offs also benefit from the inventor’s assistance in explaining the technology, answering technical questions, assessing applications, and communicating the significance of the science to potential investors, entrepreneurs, and business partners. TTOs facilitate commercialization by translating scientific insights into business plans and presentations and by connecting inventors with finance and management networks, but these activities depend on the inventor’s involvement. The faculty inventor is thus not merely the holder of a patent: they are a crucial source of tacit expertise and an indispensable participant in transferring, interpreting, validating, and commercially developing the technology.

contexts.context: The excerpt portrays tacit knowledge as highly important—often indispensable—for university technology transfer. Tacitness exists on a continuum: some knowledge is purely tacit, while other knowledge is technically codifiable but remains uncodified because codification is costly, incentives are weak, or the inventor chooses not to disclose it. Patents and publications therefore do not necessarily provide everything needed to make and use an invention; even explicit knowledge requires tacit understanding and practical know-how. This is especially significant for early-stage, novel, complex, and science-based university inventions, which often cannot fully explain their operation through formal documentation. Faculty inventors retain valuable knowledge about minor improvements, techniques, experimental procedures, and accumulated operational wisdom. Consequently, firms and university spin-offs need continuing access to the discovering scientist, not merely a patent license. The excerpt states that companies often seek invention-related tacit knowledge and that exchange between the discovering scientist and the firm is positively associated with commercialization success. The faculty inventor thus serves as a key source of know-how and practical guidance, helping the firm interpret the patent, reproduce or develop the technology, solve implementation problems, and adapt it for commercialization. Tacit knowledge may become more widely codified over time, but it is particularly crucial during the early stages of transfer.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents tacit knowledge as central to university technology transfer, rather than as a minor supplement to patents and licenses. It includes noncodified, experiential knowledge needed not only to practice an invention but also to adapt it to industrial use and commercial production. Because patents generally do not disclose this knowledge, successful transfer often requires direct, continuing interpersonal interaction between faculty inventors and commercial partners. This is especially important for spin-offs and other commercialization pathways: networks, consulting roles, sponsored research, proof-of-concept centers, incubators, and spin-offs create sustained engagement through which inventors can communicate practical know-how, assist adaptation, and help solve implementation problems that patent documents cannot convey. Such interaction also helps explain why university-industry technology transfer is often geographically localized. The faculty inventor therefore plays a role extending well beyond creating and patenting an invention: the inventor is a carrier and transmitter of experiential knowledge and may remain involved through collaboration, consulting, corporate positions, or institutional integration. The excerpt also notes that stronger academic-commercial ties can promote commercialization while raising concerns about conflicts of interest, redirected research, reduced openness, and a shift from basic toward applied research.

contexts.context: Tacit knowledge is highly important in university technology transfer because academic inventions often cannot be fully commercialized through patents or written disclosures alone. Such knowledge is difficult to codify and resides in people, institutions, and routines. Spin-offs and other commercializing firms therefore need continuing, direct interaction with academic inventors, including face-to-face communication, teaching, demonstration, training, secondment, and joint laboratory work. Simply receiving a patent or listening to a description may not provide the practical and experiential understanding needed to adapt, scale, and apply an invention. Transfer is strengthened through repeated interactions and extended relationships rather than one-off transactions; informal conversations and ongoing collaboration can progressively convey additional know-how. The faculty inventor plays a central role as a source of the invention’s tacit dimension and as an active participant in commercialization. Evidence cited in the excerpt indicates that faculty cooperation was required for successful commercialization in 71% of licensed inventions, while approximately 40% of university licenses involved faculty participation. Entrepreneurs also commonly recognize informal know-how transfer as an important output of university technology transfer. Faculty involvement can therefore help firms understand, develop, troubleshoot, and extend technologies beyond their basic patented form, although downstream firms may also contribute tacit knowledge concerning industrial scale-up and production.
